title: Does Valve approve games with AI arts generated by Canva?
author: aBigRacoon
selftext:
Hello,

I am familiar with the AI ban on Steam due to ownership claims, etc. However, while checking out the [Canva AI Product Terms](https://www.canva.com/policies/ai-product-terms/), I stumbled upon this sentence:" **Canva will not make any copyright ownership claim over your Input or Output**.  You may use your Output for any legal purpose, provided that you comply  with these terms and that you accept that any such use is at your own  risk. ". Does this mean I can show this to Valve if and when they decide to decline my game submission? 

Thanks in advance.

comments.author: artoonu
comments.body: It's not about ownership but copyright. That's why most services say "it's all up to you, we only sell processing power". As of now, legal proceedings are still not clearly settled and it all stays muddy. I did not hear of any changes from Valve's side about the matter.

comments.author: AmpedHorizon
comments.body:
I am not a legal expert and I didn't even know Canva had an image generator, but I think others can still claim that Canva used copyrighted material to train their model. So there is room for lawsuits from other artists. 

You can't claim that you own the model, so in theory it won't help to convince Valve that the model is safe to use.

comments.author: aRedJournal
comments.body:
Steam has been very explicit. They are following copyright law. 

If you are generating Batman eating a hamburger… sorry, but you don’t have the rights to that character!

replies.author: kytheon
replies.body: Banning AI assets is not in copyright law. It's a lack of a law that makes it a gray zone, and Epic and Steam choose different sides.

replies.author: aRedJournal
replies.body:
Steam says they encourage AI usage in games because they recognize the improvements in productivity. The few cases that have popped up, however, are due to copyright issues—not just the usage of AI.

Their statements have been very clear. In fact the media are directly quoting developers here on Reddit, which isn’t exactly journalistic integrity if they’re only reporting one side of the argument and without seeing the actual content that Steam has flagged internally.

replies.author: ZoopTEK
replies.body:
I ran into a strange situation myself, where \[insert big streamer\] refused to cover my game because of the existence of AI art... somewhere?  We think it was our brand new Steam capsule art, that we had JUST paid an artist to create.  The follow-up e-mail to clarify was simply ignored.

You cannot comprehend how big of a loss that was, over an incorrect allegation!

replies.author: mikebrave
replies.body:
not a single AI exists without some copyright material used as training data, even the more primitive ones like google translate are based on a huge corpus of text. 

I've always leaned toward the absence of laws against it made it legal and most cases of training on data would and should fall under fair use. 

Steam isn't doing it for copyright but rather that they know that a decisive lawsuit will happen in this space soon and they don't want to be the company that get's caught in that crossfire. Nothing ethical or legal about it, it's just dodging that particular legal hell of a bullet, which they have every right to do.

comments.author: Joewoof
comments.body: You have to use Adobe Express instead, because Adobe uses their own stock art to train their AI. Steam has stated thar they have nothing against “properly trained” AI.

replies.author: ghost_of_drusepth
replies.body: I've seen at least a couple stories from people claiming that Steam rejected their Adobe-generated art, too.

replies.author: Raradev01
replies.body: Can you point me to some examples?

comments.author: StickiStickman
comments.body: Literally just don't mention it and no one will ever know.

replies.author: StickiStickman
replies.body: Unless someone installed malware on your PC to watch you generate them, it's literally not possible.

comments.author: Lyaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa
comments.body:
Hi, even if Canva says **Canva will not make any copyright ownership claim over your Input or Output.** you aren't safe. Terms are always subject to changes.

Imagine you start a game with it, then suddenly they change their terms of use.
